style: A figure for a Nature article, drawn as a finished vector illustration on a pure white background (no grey, no paper texture, no vignette). Palette, strictly: Rose #D6336C for the method's own marks (what the model writes, its results), pale rose #F1A3BC as its tint; Cobalt #2557A7 for the strongest alternative, pale cobalt #9DB8E0; ink #1F2A44 for text and axes; blue-greys #4C5B78, #7D8BA8, #BAC5D9 for baselines and quiet structure; a very pale blue tint #F2F5FB for paper surfaces; violet #7A5BA8 only for thin dotted theory or reference lines. Typography: Helvetica Neue, small and light, sentence case, 6-8 pt at print size; mathematics set in Computer Modern italic like LaTeX. Bold lowercase panel letters a, b, c, d at the top-left of each panel. Thin hairline strokes (0.5-1 pt), generous white space, panels aligned on a shared grid with equal gutters. No frames around panels, no drop shadows, no gradients except white-ended colour ramps, no legends (labels sit at the ends of lines), no chart titles, no boxes-and-arrows flowcharts, no clip art, no robots or brains. Mood: quiet, exact, crafted, like the best figures in Nature, Quanta Magazine and Distill: one idea per panel, revealed by geometry rather than decoration. Every digit and label must be crisp and legible.

figures.prompt: Opening figure of a paper titled 'Sketchpad'. A small vision-language model (Qwen3.5, 0.8 billion parameters) does exact long arithmetic on a picture it keeps overwriting: a 'sheet' of digit cells. Its only working state is the sheet. Each 'tick' it reads a window of exactly three cells through its own vision tower and writes one digit plus the name of its next move; a fixed runtime stamps the digit and moves the window. Four panels in a 2x2 grid, 180 mm wide. Panel a (top-left, wide): a real long multiplication laid out on a pale blue-tinted paper strip in a monospaced pixel digit font: rows labelled at the left in small grey type: 'a', 'x b', 'carry x', 'carry +', 'product', 'a x b', with thin ruled lines; operand digits in dark ink, digits the model has already written in rose, and a rounded-corner outline marking the three cells being read (one cell in each of three rows of one column), the next digit about to be written glowing faintly in rose. Panel b (top-right): one tick, drawn as an optical lens or loupe hovering over the sheet: three stacked cells pass up through the lens into a slim stylised column of 24 thin horizontal layers (the network), and out of the top come exactly three tokens: a digit, a carry digit, and a letter naming the next step; drawn elegantly as light passing through glass, not as boxes and arrows. Panel c (bottom-left): a minimalist line chart, x axis 'digits' on a log scale from 10 to 1,000, y axis 'share exact' from 0 to 1; a rose line perfectly flat at 1.0 labelled 'Sketchpad' at its right end; a cobalt line falling from about 0.9 to 0 labelled 'chain of thought'; two dashed blue-grey lines falling faster, labelled at their ends. Panel d (bottom-right): a certificate: a dense grid of 2,446 tiny squares (like a woven textile or a stamp sheet), each shaded on a white-to-rose ramp by its margin, grouped into blocks for nine tables with tiny labels SUM, MUL, ADD, ADZ, FLS, NXT, SUB, EST, DEC; one square ringed in ink, marking the lowest margin, with a small annotation 'min 3.02'. A thin caption-like line under d reads 'exact on these => exact on every run'.

Figure 2 of the Sketchpad paper: 'the sheet machine', a calculator whose every digit is written by a language model reading three cells at a time. Four panels. Panel a (top row, full width): five small 'table cards' in a row, one for each operation: add (SUM), multiply (MUL), subtract (SUB), estimate a quotient digit (EST), lower the guess (DEC). Each card shows a real input view: a tall narrow strip of three stacked square cells containing monospaced pixel digits in black on white (some cells blank), and beside it, in rose, the model's answer: a digit, a second digit or a dash, and a step letter. Under each card, in tiny grey type, the size of its table (242, 1,553, 242, 400, 9). Panel b (middle-left): long division by Knuth's Algorithm D laid out on a sheet in a monospaced digit grid with ruled lines, the quotient digits written in rose, and drawn above it a thin path that walks from table to table (EST, MUL, SUB, DEC), like a route on a subway map with small round stations; a square-root sheet beside it, smaller. Panel c (middle-right): 'waves': three independent jobs drawn as three horizontal lanes of small dots (one dot per step), with vertical faint bands showing several jobs' steps sharing one forward pass; beside it a scatter of measured seconds against predicted seconds with a thin violet dotted identity line, points in rose. Panel d (bottom): a strip plot: four columns of rose dots (division, square root, gcd, signed sums), seconds on the y axis 0 to 18, a thin horizontal reference line at 12 s, and above each column '50/50 exact'.

Figure 3 of the Sketchpad paper: certification. Four panels. Panel a (top-left, the centrepiece): a designed diagram of a theorem. On the left, an unbounded branching tree of computation runs (long sums and products of any length, drawn as fine ink lines fanning out and fading to the right as they go to infinity); every node of every run is a small three-cell window. Fine threads fold each node back onto a single, compact, finite grid of views on the right (a neat rectangle of small squares). The visual message: infinitely many runs, a finite set of views; exact on the set means exact on every run. Elegant, mathematical, like a commutative diagram drawn by a designer; rose threads, ink nodes, white ground. Panel b (top-right): the counterexample: a curve of a hidden quantity that grows tick by tick, rising slowly toward a horizontal margin line, staying just under it for every test up to N and crossing it at N+1; tests up to N shown as small ticks along the x axis in cobalt; the crossing marked with a small rose cross. A second flat line shows the sheet-only machine that never crosses. Panel c (bottom-left): margins per table as nine horizontal distributions (small dot strips or violins), one row per table (SUM, MUL, ADD, ADZ, FLS, NXT, SUB, EST, DEC), x axis 'margin (logits)' from 0 to 20; each row's lowest value marked; a thin violet dotted line at zero. Panel d (bottom-right): a scatter of per-table minimum margin on the server against the same on the phone or laptop GPU, with a violet dotted identity line; rose points hug the diagonal (fp16), blue-grey points (4-bit) fall off it.

Figure 4 of the Sketchpad paper: algebra as written. A small language model factors x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 the way a textbook does, and every number in the derivation is computed on its sheet. Three panels. Panel a (left, tall, the centrepiece): the derivation typeset beautifully in LaTeX Computer Modern, line by line: the polynomial; 'candidates: 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, 6, -6'; the substitution 1^3 - 6*1^2 + 11*1 - 6 = 0; a synthetic division table with a vertical bar and a horizontal rule; '= (x - 1)(x^2 - 5x + 6)'; the discriminant; the final '(x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3)'. Every computed number is in rose, and from each rose number a hair-thin rose thread runs to the right margin, where a small column of tiny digit sheets (miniature pixel-digit column sums and products, like small receipts) shows the model's own work for that number. Panel b (top-right): refusals under planted faults: two small groups of horizontal bars or dot-and-whisker marks: 'wrong roots' 200 of 200 refused for both procedures; 'corrupted arithmetic' 92.5% (textbook, rose) against 86.5% (evaluation, cobalt), for light and strong checks. Panel c (bottom-right): seconds per work order, eleven problems on the y axis (6x6 product, linear equations, 2x2 system, expansions, quadratics, 3x3 system, factoring) with paired dots connected by a thin line: textbook in rose, evaluation in cobalt, on a log x axis, and a thin vertical line at 12 s.

Figure 5 of the Sketchpad paper: inside the model. Three panels. Panel a (left): a logit-lens heat map: rows are six tables (SUM, MUL, ADD, ADZ, FLS, NXT), columns are 24 transformer layers; each cell is the share of views whose final answer is already the top guess at that layer, white (0) to deep rose (1); the answer takes the lead abruptly at about layer 19-20, a sharp vertical edge; tiny marks above layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23 flag the full-attention layers among the gated-delta-net layers. Panel b (centre, large): the hidden state that writes the answer, as a 3D point cloud floating on white, drawn with fine perspective axes: hundreds of small dots clustered into distinct tight clouds, one per answer value 0 to 19, coloured along a cobalt-to-violet-to-rose ramp by the value, each cluster's numeral printed beside it in small type; a faint curve threads the cluster centres in order, like a number line bent in space. A smaller second cloud for multiplication. Panel c (right): a dose-response style line chart: x axis 'layer of the push' 4 to 22, y axis 'share of steps changed' 0 to 1; a rose curve flat near zero then jumping to 1 at layer 20, a blue-grey dashed curve that stays low; a thin violet vertical dotted line at layer 19 labelled 'full attention'.

Figure 6 of the Sketchpad paper: one model that decides. Three panels. Panel a (left): the gate, drawn as a designed schematic, not boxes and arrows: a single weight matrix W drawn as a fine grid, with a thin low-rank side path (two slender matrices A and B, the adapter) running parallel to it, joining back through a small dial or valve labelled with a gate value g; at g = 0 the side path is dark and the model is stock, bit for bit; at g = 1 it carries the sheet machine. The equation y = xW + g(xA^T)B^T set in LaTeX beneath. Two tiny insets: '2,500 / 2,500 chat calls identical' and '2,688 / 2,688 table rows identical'. Panel b (centre): a scatter: x axis 'GSM8K, points vs stock', y axis 'IFEval, points vs stock', stock at the origin as an open ink circle; five chat runs P2, P3, P4, P5 and a 'gate switch' run as rose dots, connected in order by a thin line that shows a seesaw: improving one axis costs the other; a pale rose shaded rectangle marks the region where both bars pass (above -2 on both). Panel c (right): precision and recall of opening the sheet: a small slope chart or paired dots, stock few-shot in cobalt (0.971 / 0.809) and the runs in rose near 1.0.

A single elegant scientific illustration: a long strip of pale paper with rows of monospaced digits (a long multiplication), seen slightly from above; over one column hovers a thin circular glass lens (like a jeweller's loupe drawn in fine lines) that isolates exactly three stacked cells; above the lens, the three cells reappear magnified and pass into a slim vertical column of 24 thin translucent layers, and out of the top emerge three small tokens: '7', '3', and the letter 'A', the digit '7' in rose. To the left of the lens the digits already written are rose; to the right the paper is still blank. Fine line art with flat fills, no photorealism, white background.

A single elegant mathematical diagram on white: an infinite fan of computation traces (thin ink polylines of different lengths, some very long, fading toward the right edge, labelled n = 10, n = 100, n = 1,000 ...) whose every vertex is a tiny three-cell window; from each vertex, a hair-thin rose thread falls down onto a finite, compact grid of small squares at the bottom (the set of all possible windows, 2,446 of them), so that the infinite set of runs folds onto the finite set of views like a projection. A typeset statement beneath in Computer Modern: 'exact on every view  <=>  exact on every run'. Quiet, crafted, like a Quanta Magazine illustration of a theorem.

Opening figure of a Nature paper, 180 mm wide, three full-width rows on a pure white background. Row 1, the mechanism, one designed piece across the width: on the left a filmstrip of three small frames of the same long-multiplication sheet at three consecutive steps (monospaced pixel digits on a very pale blue-tinted paper, row labels 'a', 'x b', 'carry x', 'carry +', 'product', 'a x b' tight in the left margin, thin ruled lines; in each frame a rounded ink outline marks the three cells being read, and the digit the model just wrote is rose while earlier writing is pale rose). On the right, one step at token level: a tall thin strip of three pixel cells (32 x 96 pixels, black on white) passes through a small patch-grid glyph (the vision encoder, 16-pixel patches merged 2 x 2) into three image-token boxes in a prompt row of small rounded token boxes 'MUL [img] [img] [img] = ? ?'; above the row, 24 thin horizontal slabs stacked like sheets of glass, six of them darker (full attention); above '=' and the two '?' slots three answer tokens in rose: a digit, a carry digit and the letter of the next step. A single hairline joins the window in the last frame to the strip. Row 2, the guarantee: a compact mosaic of 2,446 tiny squares grouped by table (MUL, SUM, ADD, ADZ, SUB, EST, NXT, FLS, DEC), shaded white to rose by margin, with a callout to the weakest square showing its real pixels and 'margin 3.02', and one clean typeset line: 'exact on all 2,446 views => exact on every run of every length (Theorem 1)'. Row 3, the result, full width: a clean benchmark bar chart like a model release, one horizontal bar per system (Sketchpad 100% in rose marked 'certified', GPT-6.1 Sol in cobalt, Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5, gpt-oss-120b, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, Gemma 4 31B, Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3.5-0.8B in blue-grey), values at the bar ends, quiet italic group labels (frontier, open, Qwen3.5), and beside them two narrow bar columns for the hardest cells, '+ 1,000 digits' and 'x 20 digits'. One type scale, 6-7 pt labels, no frames, no gridlines, generous but even gutters. Emphasise a strict grid: every panel edge aligned, equal gutters, nothing floating.

A close, exact technical illustration of one step of a vision-language model at token level, white background, Cobalt and Rose palette: a tall thin strip of three cells of black pixel digits '8', '1', '0' (32 x 96 pixels, visible pixel grid), overlaid by a 2 x 6 grid of 16-pixel patches, merged 2 x 2 into three image tokens; a horizontal row of small rounded token boxes 'MUL', three image tokens, '=', '?', '?'; above it 24 very thin stacked horizontal slabs, six darker; above '=' and the two '?' boxes the answers '8', '0', 'A' in rose with tiny labels 'digit', 'carry', 'next step'. Minimal, Distill-like, precise, no ellipses, no arrows, hairline connectors only.
